description: Hi! My name is Daniil Semenov, and I’m 11 years old. I’ve been interested in STEM for several years, especially robotics, electronics, and coding. This is my second year taking part in FIRST LEGO League, and I’m also a Science Leader at my school. I can program using the Arduino IDE and enjoy building things and solving problems. This is my second NASA Space Apps Challenge, and I’m excited to take part independently, develop my skills, and aim for an award this year!
summary:
I developed Red Dust Outpost, an interactive Mars survival game for the NASA Space Apps Junior Astronaut Program. Players act as Junior Commanders keeping four astronauts alive for 12 sols until resupply arrives.
To make complex space logistics accessible to kids, we replaced complicated math with a simple daily loop across five gauges: oxygen, power, water, food, and shielding. Every choice—like splitting water for air or charging solar panels—reflects real aerospace science, including ISS electrolysis, dust storms, and Earth communication delays.
This teaches young learners critical thinking and real-world space exploration constraints through intuitive, engaging play.
details: Red Dust Outpost — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a turn-based Mars survival strategy game built on Base44 (using modern web technologies like React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge that challenges players to keep four astronauts alive for 12 Martian sols until a resupply ship arrives. Designed so children as young as seven can play independently after one round without heavy math or spreadsheets, the game follows a simple four-step daily loop where players read a Mission Control briefing, spend a single crew action to manage interconnected resources (like splitting water into oxygen, charging batteries, or patching radiation shielding), watch how planetary events shift their telemetry gauges, and read one-line explanations for every change. Its creative strength lies in translating real NASA and ISS constraints—such as water electrolysis, dust storms blocking solar panels, solar flare radiation, and 5-to-20-minute Earth communication delays—into accessible, high-stakes trade-offs inside an authentic mission-control interface. When designing the project, we carefully balanced scientific accuracy with low cognitive load and constructive failure logs, aiming to build systems-thinking skills, resilience, and early excitement for space exploration among young learners.
